articles.text: Piedmont City Council interviewed applicants and made appointments to the Measure UU Pool Bond Oversight Committee at a special meeting held on December 13, 2021. The council appointed former mayor John Chiang, Margaret Hiller, Al Lee, Patricia Leicher, and Dirk ten Grotenhuis to serve on this committee. Leicher will be committee’s chair. The committee members bring with them years of professional experience in accounting, regulatory auditing, public fiduciary oversight, and financial and executive management. The ad-hoc committee will meet twice a year and will terminate when the expenditure of the bond proceeds is complete. A requirement of general obligation bond Measure UU, passed by voters in November 2020 to build a new community pool, is to establish a bond oversight committee. The committee will inform the public on how the city is expending the bond proceeds and review expenditure reports produced by the city. Committee members will produce an annual report which will include a statement indicating whether the bonds used are appropriate as set forth in Measure UU, and a summary of the committee’s proceedings and actives for the preceding year. The Bond Oversight Committee is not responsible for managing or directing any pool activities; instead, it will leverage the experience and expertise of its members to ensure bond proceeds are spend in accordance with Ordinance 754 N.S., or Measure UU. articles.text: Recently, Oakland City Council Member Abel Guillen’s office called asking if I would be able to serve as the moderator at a meeting that evening between the Council Member, Oakland Human Services Director Sarah Bedford, Assistant City Administrator Joe Devries and members of the community concerning the city’s plan to move the homeless persons living in tents around Lake Merritt to “Community Cabins”(Tuff Sheds) located on the parking lot of the old Kaiser Auditorium at the south end of the lake. Wishing I could honestly say “I would love to but I have a previous commitment,” but unable to do so, I agreed to be there. When the meeting started there were brief introductions, short preliminary statements and I was introduced as the one who would manage the heart of the meeting. It would consist of questions from the gathered community and responses from the city officials. The sanctuary of the church was filled to overflowing. I restated the purpose of the evening – a better understanding of the city’s response to a complex and heart-rending situation, invited everyone to speak in a manner that they would like to be spoken to, and promised that I would give the microphone to as many questioners as time would allow before we came to the end of our allotted time in the building. As predicted, the questioning was intense and the concern for the well-being of the unhoused on the part of their spokespersons, the residents who live around the lake and the city officials genuine. The often repeated themes were: 1. the number of unhoused persons in Oakland is high, approximately 3,000 on any given evening 2. public land must remain available to the public for the purposes to which it is dedicated 3. the city is committed to lifting people up rather than forcing them out 4. the amount of resources available to address this humanitarian crisis is increasing but the needs remain great; there is debate about how those resources should best be allocated. As the time to end the meeting approached I allotted time for a few questions, gave the responders an opportunity to make brief closing statements and ended the meeting by saying “Thank you all for speaking your truth. Lives hang in the balance. May the promises made come to fruition. Peace be upon us all as we leave this sacred place.” I wish I could say that I left

articles.text: The Piedmont City Council will hold a special meeting on Thursday, January 6 to discuss the process for appointing a successor to council member Tim Rood, who resigned on December 31, 2021. The council will provide direction to staff as to what method of appointment will be used to fill the vacancy. Rood resigned due to his new residence being in Oakland, making him ineligible to serve on Piedmont’s City Council. Rood made the announcement of his resignation on December 20, 2021. When a seat is vacated on Piedmont’s City Council for any reason, the city’s Charter dictates that, within 60 days of vacancy, city council members must appoint a successor who will serve on an interim basis until residents vote for a replacement at the next general municipal election. If the vacancy is not filled by March 1, it will be filled by special election. That appointee will serve until the results of the general municipal election of November 2022 is certified, according to a staff report authored by City Administrator Sara Lillevand released yesterday, January 4. The council has two options to fill the vacancy. It may select and appoint a qualified resident, or may open applications to the public and interview applicants. City Clerk John Tulloch confirmed that in the previous two appointments, in 2016 and 2017, the city council chose the latter method. A person must meet three criteria to serve on Piedmont City Council: • must be a qualified voter in the city • must not hold any other office or employment in the city • must not be rendered ineligible due to the term limits provisions of the City Charter. The appointee may run for two full terms on the council.
articles.title: City Council special meeting Jan. 6 to determine process for replacing Rood

articles.text: Piedmont City Council voted unanimously at its most recent meeting, December 20, 2021, to adopt an update to the Piedmont Sustainable Procurement Policy, formally named the Environmentally Preferable Purchasing Policy. Updates to the policy intend to encourage and increase the use of environmentally sustainable products and services in Piedmont whenever practical. Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman and Climate Action Fellow Annie Wensley provided information to council members detailing the major changes in the policy. California Senate Bill 1383 (SB 1383), signed into law in 2016, requires city council members, city and county boards, and other highlevel decision makers to start planning and implementing programs that reduce “short-lived” climate pollutants. SB 1383 regulations went into effect on January 1, 2022. Dykman explained that the adoption of requirements set by SB 1383, in addition to updates presented by the city’s Sustainability Department, help Piedmont reach ambitious goals set by Climate Action Plan 2.0. “We’re looking toward ways to making municipal practices more sustainable, and here we have SB 1383, being the impetus to push us over the finish line to get these updates in place,” Dykman said. Updates to the policy will allow purchasing of materials, including compostable or recyclable materials, to be cost-effective, and will demonstrate to the public that ‘green’ or sustainable purchasing practices are efficient. All purchases made by the city must be “durable, long-lasting, reusable, or refillable,” according to a staff report authored by Dykman and Wensley. Electronic distribution of documents, rather than ‘hard-copies,’ will be encouraged. Wherever applicable, energy-efficient equipment shall be purchased with most up-to-date energy efficient functions, among various other updates that solidify the city’s goals and efforts in sustainable practices. “Staff will meet with department heads on a regular basis to assess progress of implementation, and develop an internal purchasing guide and recording keeping system,” Wensley added.
articles.title: City Council OKs Sustainable Procurement Policy

Updates to the policy intend to encourage and increase the use of environmentally sustainable products and services in Piedmont whenever practical. Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman and Climate Action Fellow Annie Wensley provided information to council members detailing the major changes in the policy. Over the past 12 months we’ve worked to identify and evaluate options for replacement of our aging system,” said Police Chief Jeremy Bowers. A beta test of a new camera vendor, Flock Safety, was conducted at the intersections of Blair and Calvert Avenues and Kingston and Linda Avenues last year. The same vendor has been successfully utilized in several Bay Area municipalities, including Vallejo, Benicia, Pittsburg, and Walnut Creek. The proposal allows the Piedmont police to cover more locations on the city’s borders with technology that identifies stolen vehicles entering and leaving the city. Chief Bowers explained to City Council members that although the technology does not identify the driver or passenger, those who drive vehicles reported stolen are more likely to commit other crimes, such as catalytic converter thefts. “We’re covering areas that we know, based on experience, are ‘holes’ that existed in our boundaries and borders,” said Chief Bowers. “We’ll still have ingress Piedmont’s City Council approved an agreement for license plate readers with a new vendor, Flock Safety, at a December 20 meeting. and egress [locations], but we will focus more on ingress [of vehicles].” Bowers confirmed that his department is aware of the continued security and privacy concerns related to ALPR technology and added that facial recognition technology is not used by the department and was not being proposed. ALPR cameras capture images of license plates and do not record video. In addition, only approved department staff are authorized to access the Flock Safety system and each access must contain their unique identifier, password, and the investigative reason for their access. “[This technology] gives us more of a data-driven approach to locating criminal activity. At the end of the day, it’s about the relationship the law enforcement agency has with the community it is serving,” Bowers added. “I appreciate Flock Safety for their awareness of that need between a community and its police department.” Bowers also cited the department’s transparency portal, one of the first of its kind in the country, as a tool residents may use for more information. articles.text: A Special School Board meeting will be held on Thursday, January 6, to approve a 2.5% increase in teachers’ salaries. It is based upon a collective bargaining tentative agreement between Piedmont School District and the teachers’ union. The meeting will be available on Zoom at Zoom.us/j/88990644177 and will be held in City Hall starting at 9:30 a.m. The raises will be retroactive to July 1, 2021. Last year’s summer school salaries and the entire 2021-2022 salaries will include the increase. Elise Marks, president of the Associate Piedmont Teachers, explained the basis of retroactive raises. “Last spring, when state funding seemed dismal, APT and CSEA agreed to have the district hold back some Measure H money to deal with shortfalls. Over the summer, the state funding situation improved dramatically. That’s why we came back to the table in November,” she said. The raises will cause an increase in the district’s expenditures by $528,205, for this current year. An increase in salaries of $544,488 is expected for the 2022-23 year and $549,946 for 2023-24. The cumulative cost of the settlement is $1,622,638. Marks expressed gratitude for district’s effort to compensate its faculty but cautioned that the cost of living for teachers is “rising perilously fast.” “APT is incredibly grateful to the community for Measure H, but we need the community to know that even with this 2.5% increase, our salaries are still falling behind inflation. The Legislative Analyst’s Office is predicting inflation of 5.35% for next year, and teachers are very worried,” Marks explained. Measure H was approved by voters in 2019 to recruit and retain educators and is the source of the raises. At the last board meeting the board approved the updated December budget, which showed $1,000,000 left over from the 2021 calendar year due to increases in state and federal funding. The new expenditures for teacher salaries will not require budget revisions for this year according to the district. The terms of the new agreement for teachers will be incorporated as part of the District’s 2021-2022 Adopted Budget and multi-year projections. The tentative agreement includes new and updated language in the following article: • Article XVI: Salaries Article XVI Salaries P. The salary schedule in Appendix A shall reflect a 2.5% increase in the daily rate over the initial schedule of 2021-2022 and reflect an annual salary for 185 days. This increase shall be applied retroactively to July 1, 2021.

In an effort to ensure that students and faculty can return to school safely today, Wednesday January 5, Piedmont School District offered students the opportunity to pick up at-home Covid-19 test kits last week at the district office and at Havens School. The kits were part of six million test kits provided by the California Department of Public Health to all public and charter schools. Piedmont received 3,000 kits from the state, with two tests per kit. Roughly 2,600 were distributed to families of students and PUSD staff. The city of Piedmont set a record on December 31, 2021, with 48 confirmed new Covid cases on a single day. articles.text: PHS loses to Encinal, Oakland HS before Christmas break Staff Photos Jason Harris (left) takes over the boys’ basketball interim head coach after Ben Spencer stepped aside to focus on his young family. Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team has seen a big change at the helm. Head coach Ben Spencer announced that he is stepping aside to focus on his family after the recent birth of his son, Jordan. He is handing over the reigns to assistant coaches Jason Harris and Shamaree Worley; Harris will lead on an interim basis, while Worley will continue as his first assistant. “It’s a bit of a moving target, but we’re just stepping in until Ben can fully come back. There’s not an exact date on it, but we’re progressing as if we’ll be going forward like this for the rest of the season. It’s a tough situation,” said Harris. A coaching change is not easy for a young roster. Piedmont High walked into its Winter Break with a 4-7 record after two losses in two days to Encinal on December 17, and Oakland HS on December 18. Being without senior leader JoJo Murphy due to injury has directly contributed to the game results. Junior A.J. Harris, the son of coach Harris and current scoring leader, has been the target of consistent double coverage by opposing defenses. “JoJo’s injury and Ben stepping aside is obviously a lot to overcome. We’re built around JoJo and A.J., so taking one of them out is very difficult when playing a hard schedule,” explained coach Harris. “Northgate (10-2 overall) is ranked, Saint Ignatius (9-1 overall) is ranked, Campolindo (9-1 overall) is a top-50 team in the country, and we’ve played Oakland (14-1 overall) twice. It’s been a tough schedule,” he added. The two-week school break over Christmas couldn’t have come at a better time; Murphy has trained hard to be at full strength for their returns tonight against Berkeley. Their coach, Mike Hudson, was Murphy’s coach at Piedmont when he was a freshman in 2018-19. “JoJo’s been back and we’ve gotten back to our core of moving the ball unselfishly. We’re used to being a really great offensive team, and it hasn’t been that way. Assistant Shamaree Worley will continue coaching with Harris. We’ve been spending a lot of time on driving, kicking out, and moving the ball. They really practiced great last week and I’m excited about the progress,” said coach Harris. Harris originally was an assistant coach under former coach Chris Lavdiotis 15 years ago until taking time to focus on his family and career. He returned as the freshman coach in 2017 under Mike Hudson, managed the Junior Varsity program in 2018, and then became Spencer’s assistant varsity coach in 2019. Harris played basketball at Hamilton College in 1993. Coach Worley played at De Anza HS and collegiately at College of Marin and Simpson College in Iowa. Both coaches were with Spencer when Piedmont won the first North Coast Section championship in school history in March 2020. “We’re focused on not worrying about our record or ranking and having a good practice every day and working toward improving. We can all get better; it’s a team effort for coaches and players. Things will fall into place when you practice great,” said Harris.

Typically ranging from November through February, the common Coccinellidae beetle is annually called to the fence posts and plants residing along the Stream Trail at Redwood Regional. “Here in Redwood, ladybugs wait out the winter, often along the creeks,” explained East Bay Regional Parks in describing the phenomenon. “They are likely attracted to the area by chemicals in the air, or from pheromones, or scent markers, left behind in their footprints.” About 1.5 miles down the Stream Trail are bushels of ladybugs. articles.text: Photo courtesy of NFL.com John Madden passed away at the age of 85 on December 28. He was head coach of the Oakland Raiders from 1969-1978, and was inducted into the NFL Hall of Fame in 2006. The National Football League announced on December 28 that former Raiders head coach John Madden, a longtime East Bay resident, passed away at the age of 85. “On behalf of the entire NFL family, we extend our condolences to Virginia, Mike, Joe and their families,” said NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell in a press release. “We all know him as the Hall of Fame coach of the Oakland Raiders and broadcaster who worked for every major network, but more than anything, he was a devoted husband, father and grandfather. “Nobody loved football more than Coach. He was football. He was an incredible sounding board to me and so many others. There will never be another John Madden, and we will forever be indebted to him for all he did to make football and the NFL what it is today.” Madden’s career was extended as a popular broadcaster for CBS, FOX, ABC and NBC for 30 years. The popular “Madden NFL” video game became the most popular sports game of all time. Both his broadcasting and video game franchise attracted countless young minds to the game of football, including this writer. His hilarious commentary was sometimes obvious, simplifying the game known for its complexity at the pro level. “If the quarterback throws the ball in the end zone, and the receiver catches it, it’s a touchdown,’ said Madden in previous broadcasts, via USA Today. Madden was drafted by the Philadelphia Eagles in the 21st round during the 1958 draft. He suffered a knee injury that ended his playing career and led to him to pursue coaching. He spent four years at Hancock College in Santa Maria, California. before being hired as defensive coordinator at San Diego State. The Raiders later hired Madden as their linebackers coach in 1967 and eventually promoted him to head coach for the 1969 season. During his career, Madden led the Raiders to a record of 103-32-7 (76.3 percent), including the Super Bowl title in 1976, and becoming perhaps the most prolific coach in the team’s history. The culture of his years at the helm from 1969-1978 still brands the organization throughout its time in Oakland, Los Angeles, and now Las Vegas. He was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2006.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco Judy Chicago ‘On Fire at 80,’ 2019; archival inkjet print. A retrospective art exhibit celebrating the pioneering feminist artist Judy Chicago is now on display at the de Young Museum in San Francisco. The exhibit will be on display until this Sunday, January 9. Judy Chicago is one of the founding figures behind the 1970’s feminist art movement. Her storied career is highlighted through her colorful works on canvas, porcelain plates, car hoods and more. The exhibition will include approximately 130 paintings, prints, drawings and sculptures by the artist. The exhibit is organized in conjunction with the 100th anniversary of women’s right to vote in the United States, and pays homage to Judy Chicago who fought against the suppression of women’s creativity. She founded the first feminist arts education program in the country at California State University in Fresno. To purchase tickets to the exhibition, visit https://deyoung.famsf. org/exhibitions/judy-chicago. ®

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse presents its production of Twelfth Night running now through January 15. Twelfth Night was named one of the best theatrical productions of 2018 by Time Magazine, The Hollywood Reporter and The Washington Post. The play is a contemporary musical adaption of William Shakespeare’s classic romantic comedy about mistaken identity and eventual self-discovery. Viola washes up on the shores of Illyria on the twelfth day of Christmas disguised as a man who eventually falls for a Duke – Viola navigates the gender confusion in her role while she finds her true love in the process. San Francisco Playhouse’s production and interpretation of the Shakespeare classic features an original jazz-funk score by Shania Taub. To purchase tickets and for show times, visit: https://www.sfplayhouse.org/sfph/upcoming-plays/. Proof of vaccination against COVID-19 is required to attend the production.
articles.title: SF Playhouse’s Twelfth Night on view through January 15

articles.text: Marin Theatre Company will present its first production of the year, Pass Over, beginning January 27 and with performances through February 20. Pass Over is Antoinette Chinoye Nwandu’s new play, directed by Kevin R. Free. The play casts Edward Ewell as Moses, LeRoy S. Graham as Kitch, and Adam Roy as Mister. Moses and Kitch pass the time and dream of their version of a promised land when a stranger wanders into their space and disrupts their plans. The play crafts everyday profanities into poetic and humorous rifts. To obtain tickets visit: https:// www.marintheatre.org/productions/pass-over-1#overview. Marin Theatre is located at 397 Miller Avenue in Mill Valley; phone number is (415) 388-5200. Proof of vaccination and masking is required. Playwright Antoinette Chinoye Nwandu

The first video stream to be offered is the Danish String Quartet’s performances of Schubert’s String Quartet in G major, available to stream January 13 through January 19. Live performances will still take place in front of audiences in Zellerbach Hall on the UC Berkeley campus. The at-home series serves as an expansion of the season’s programming. “While we will continue to focus our primary efforts on creating the highest caliber of live performances for the remainder of this season, not all of our felLive shows will still be performed at Zellerbach Hall by Cal Performances, and at-home streaming services will expand this season’s programming. low arts supporters have felt comfortable coming back to in-person performances,” said Artistic Director Jeremy Geffen. “These recordings are valuable because they allow us to share the joy of these exceptional performances with even more people in our community, including those who are still hesitant to return to live performances.” More details about the streaming series and registration to watch videos can be found at calperformances.org/at-home. articles.text: San Francisco Symphony announced updated safety protocols on January 4 for audiences attending live performances at Davies Symphony Hall. Beginning February 1, proof of a COVID-19 booster received at least one week prior to an event will be required for entrances into the symphony hall. The announcement expands the symphony’s already established requirement that all patrons, performers, volunteers, and staff age 12 and up present proof of vaccination against COVID-19 for entry into Davies Symphony Hall and all events held at that venue. Audience members younger than 12 may show proof of vaccination or a negative COVID-19 test. Audience members age 2 to 4 must show proof of a negative COVID-19 test. PCR tests may be shown within 48 hours of the event, or a antigen rapid test shown within 24 hours of the event. Full vaccination is defined by the Centers for Disease Control as the competition of the twodose vaccine series of Pfizer or Moderna, and one dose of Johnson & Johnson. Up-to-date vaccination is defined as two weeks following full initial vaccination until eligible to receive a booster, and for those eligible, one week after receiving a booster. These protocols follow policies enacted by San Francisco Department of Public Health. Further details about health and safety protocols can be found at www.sfsymphony.org/home/ safety. Tickets for upcoming events may be purchased online at www.sfsymphony.org or by calling the Box Office at 415- 864-6000. Davies Symphony Hall
articles.title: SF Symphony to require current vaccinations

articles.text: Sa n Fr a n c i s c o Ba l le t announced yesterday, January 4, that the 2022 Season Gala will be postponed to March 24 due to the resurgence of the Omicron COVID-19 variant. The 89th Repertory Season Gala was scheduled to take place at the War Memorial Opera House and San Francisco City Hall on January 27. The annual gala did not take place last year due to the COVID pandemic. This year’s gala includes the world premieres of ballets by Alexei Ratmansky, Yuri Possokhov, and Myles Thatcher, plus the stage premiere of a pas de deux from Danielle Rowe’s Wooden Dimes. “For nearly 90 years, San Francisco Ballet has contributed to the cultural richness of the Bay Area and has served as an ambassador for the city around the world and as a dedicated community member at home,” said Interim Executive Director Danielle St. Germain-Gordon. “For 37 of those years, [Artistic Director] Helgi Tomasson has been an exemplary leader for our company and community. We are thrilled to be coming back to live performances and celebrating the joy of ballet in person, gathering our community in support of our mission, and expressing our eternal gratitude to Helgi for his historic leadership and our excitement to celebrate his legacy for the entire 2022 season.” Gala dinner ticketholders and performance-only ticketholders are entitled to admission to the rescheduled 2022 Season Gala on Thursday, March 24. Gala Photo by Eric Tomasson dinner ticketholders may contact the Special Events Office at specialevents@sfballet.org to donate tickets if they prefer, exchange them into a special event later in the 2022 Season, or request a refund by February 1. Patrons who purchased Gala performance-only tickets and wish to exchange them for a different performance during the 2022 Season or request a refund should contact Ticket Services at 415-865-2000 or by emailing tickets@sfballet. org by February 1.
articles.title: SF Ballet reschedules Gala to March 24 due to COVID

articles.text: Did you ever meet the man who knew everything? Don’t jump to conclusions, since you are probably reading this column on January 5. No, I am not speaking of the Alfred Hitchcock movie nor the man who pretends to be the smartest man in the room…That guy becomes president of the United States. I am speaking of the real deal; a guy who really knew everything. I knew someone like this. So, let me tell you about him. Prepare to be inspired. People who know the name Mario Frosali are violinists. That’s because Frosali was one of the best violin makers of the 20th century. As you can surmise he was a northern Italian, thus, he spoke two languages from the very beginning. The local dialect is actually a separate language, but he also spoke French and musically-accented English. Frosali really wanted to be an artist not a musician, but his father tricked him and entered him in the Milan Conservatory. He made his first violin at age 10 and was still at the violin maker’s bench at the age of 95. His reputation was sterling – great violins and complete honesty. That says something about the man. But violin making was not his main profession. He was a respected teacher and an important orchestra conductor. While conducting the orchestra in New York’s Biltmore Hotel, he got to know four presidents of the United States – Theodore Roosevelt, William Howard Taft, Woodrow Wilson, and the popular Warren Harding. The musical connections are even more interesting, and Frosali’s musical lineage is fascinating. Giacomo Puccini was a regular guest in the Frosali home, and young Mario knew Puccini‘s teacher also. That places us way back in the 1830s. Along the way were friendships with immortals like Fritz Kreisler and Jascha Heifetz. It was Heifetz who told me that Frosali was his violin maker in New York in the 1930s. Frosali told me many things about Heifetz. What a connection that was. Frosali was a great teacher, like a musical and ethical Socrates – literally a living encyclopedia. The interesting thing is that I never paid Frosali for a lesson. All this information was freely given – a musical epiphany, if you will. If you are reading this column on Thursday, January 6, know that it is Frosali‘s birthday, going way back to 1886. Famed violin maker Mario Frosali.

articles.text: Little George Benson’s stepfather got him started on a ukulele and played a lot of Benny Goodman sextet recordings with the first notable bop guitarist, Charlie Christian. GB thinks vocally, as expressed with his scat singing. Thus, he has a great “ear” and is able to easily exchange ideas from the fretboard to his musical imagination and back to the guitar. He carefully learned Charlie Christian’s style, often based on “held” arpeggios, where the notes of a chord are fretted simultaneously as you pick through individual notes. GB’s style is based on blues, R&B and swing music. He uses mixtures of pentatonic scales like T-Bone Walker and B.B. King. Like Charlie Christian and Nat King Cole’s guitar player Oscar Moore, GB uses a strong arpeggio basis (chords playing one note at-a-time). first album as a leader, “The New Boss Guitar of George Benson”, he had adopted attributes from fellow Philadelphian guitarists: the cool smoothness of Grant Green and the blazing fast sixteenth notes of Pat Martino. third album, “George Benson Cookbook”, he had added chromatic melody he picked up from Charlie Parker. The Charlie Christian and Charlie Parker influences added bebop to GB’s playing. Bebop chromaticizing is designed to put chord tones on the beat. Or, with a “push” a chord tone can be played immediately before a beat, then leaving a Jazz guitarist George Benson silence on the beat that follows. In scat singing (jazz vocalization), this “push” note is pronounced “bop”, while the other notes are pronounced “be” or “ba”. Hence the name “bebop”. Slurred notes (two pitched in one breath) in scat singing can be pronounced “bwah”. The technical explanation in this paragraph is complex. Read the following Guitar Improv chapter to get a more detailed explanation: http://www.guitarimprov.com/zc-Chromaticized_ Scales_on_Arpeggios.pdf With scalar chromatics, one or two consecutive chromatic tones can ascend toward a target chord tone, with a delayed resolution by then descending one or two chromatics from above the target, then finally the target. If either of the tones approaching from above the target are not harmonically acceptable with the current chord scale tones a half step higher can be used. A very likable attribute of GB’s style is his alternating from high range to low range. This can easily be seen and heard in the Donna Lee-Benson Bop example, which is my improvisation in GB’s style. articles.text: Chappaquiddick is a surprisingly intense, carefully paced and meticulously crafted film that examines an accident and its aftermath, one involving Senator Edward Kennedy, aka Ted/Teddy, and a 28-year-old campaign staffer, Mary Jo Ko Kopechne, who worked for the recently assassinated Bobby Kennedy. The year is 1969. The setting is Martha’s Vineyard where the Senator and aides are hosting a dinner for the women who are referred to as “the Boiler Room Girls.” The gathering is meant to express gratitude by the Kennedy family for their hard work in the late Senator’s campaign for president. Though never expressed overtly, there is an attraction between Teddy (Jason Clarke) and Mary Jo (Kate Mara). At some point in the evening, Teddy suggests that the two of them drive to the beach, and they leave the dinner. The Senator drives (though he has been drinking), and Mary Jo sits quietly in the passenger-seat. It’s dark, the country road narrow, and they take a wrong turn heading not to the Ferry or the beach but down a dusty lane leading to a wooden bridge with a channel pond just below. Teddy misjudges the entrance onto the bridge and the car plunges into the shallow water landing upside down. Somehow Kennedy manages to escape from the flooding car. He’s never able to explain how, and later insists that he made numerous attempts to extract Mary Jo from the car. Failing to find her, he swims to the edge of the pond where he sits for some 15 minutes staring at the submerged car. It’s at that point that Chappaquiddick becomes a character study of a famous politician who is nurturing presidential aspirations, and how he confronts what is initially viewed as a tragedy. He inexplicably makes one decision after another that, in the aggregate, reveal him to be unable to act with integrity. It’s a bleak portrait, and as events begin to take shape, the word “inexplicable” frames all that follows the accident. Thought there is a house only Jason Clarke portrays Ted Kennedy in Chappaquiddick. yards from the bridge and submerged car, Kennedy walks back to the cottage where the party is still ongoing. He finds his cousin, Joe Gargan (Ed Helms), and U.S. Attorney Paul Markham (Jim Gaffigan), and they drive back to the bridge where the two men dive to attempt to get the car doors open. They also fail. They tell Kennedy that he must immediately report the accident and he agrees, and then leaves them, returning to his hotel room where he crawls into bed and falls asleep. The next morning he gets up and has brunch with friends. Finally, some 10 hours after the accident, he reports what happened to the local police. Meanwhile there are flashes of Mary Jo, her face pressed against the roof of the car where an air pocket has formed, trying to breathe and calling out the Senator’s name. These scenes create the assumption that she was alive and desperate for hours post-accident and could have been saved. After Kennedy delivers a written statement to the police, he returns to Hyannis Port and the Kennedy compound where a circle of advisors arrive and begin the unconscionable process of creating a narrative of how and why the Senator was in that car with Mary Jo and why it took hours before he sought help. It is an awful depiction of these men, Kennedy’s enablers, as they polish Ted’s story to a high gloss, portraying him as a victim. Stunningly, Kopechne is all but ignored while her parents are lost in grief and silence. This film is painful to watch, though it’s never melodramatic. It is studied and deliberate, allowing the timeline to evolve, hour after hour, revealing Kennedy to be a man who seems to have been followed most of his life by others who have taken responsibility for his bad choices and ultimately asked to fix them. At one point Joe Gargan is referred to as Kennedy’s “fixer”. Embedded in the story is the question of who are these people whose public personas disguise the individual behind the mask? And why are we perpetually surprised when they are revealed to have feet not of marble but clay? There is also the issue of redemption. Kennedy was repeatedly chosen by the people of Massachusetts to be their Senator, allowing him to spend the next 40 years in Congress where he became known as “the Lion of the Senate.” Were those four decades of hard work and service a tenacious and unyielding search for personal forgiveness? The Senator, the last of the Kennedy brothers, never fully explained how that tragic accident shaped the rest of his life. Chappaquiddick. Directed by John Curran. Starring Jason Clarke, Kate Mara, Bruce Dern. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated PG-13.

articles.text: After reviewing more than a few kids’ movies, animated and live/action, or features with a seamless blending (thanks to CGI technology) of both, I’ve become well acquainted with the extraordinary art and imaginative storytelling that’s involved in animated features. I find that I must remind myself who the targeted audience is. That would be those young budding film critics, some dedicated cinephiles, who are, when push comes to shove, content to be told a good story, one with solid visuals, while they remain ever forgiving when animals (or giant reptiles) take on distinctly human characteristics (e.g. speech or expressions). The Good Dinosaur, a Disney-Pixar film, fits nicely in the above framework. The narrative focuses on a young dinosaur named Arlo (Raymond Ochoa). He falls into a raging river and is knocked out, and when he awakens he finds that he is a long way from home and in distress. He realizes that he is separated from his family, Poppa Henry (Jeffrey Wright) and Momma Ida (Frances McDormand). With the help of a feral, street-wise (so to speak) pre-verbal Neanderthal cave boy (Jack Bright), called Spot, who can snarl and howl with the best, the two set out on a harrowing journey. The ultimate wish is merely to be reunited with home and family. Along the way they meet a menagerie of creatures, some friendly, others not so much. And there are also obstacles to overcome. For the young audience to enjoy The Good Dinosaur it’s not necessary to be able to identify the cohort of dinos that the duo meet in their travels, each having a salad of vowels and consonants as part of their names, examples being velociraptors and pterodactyls. They also encounter a family of T-Rex ranchers, led by Butch (Sam Elliot plus his cowpoke partners). The story is a simple one and follows a familiar formula that kids will find familiar, yet nevertheless entertaining. As expected, it has a right ending for both Spot and Arlo, reminding kids that the fun is in the journey as well as the destination. The Good Dinosaur. Directed by Peter Sohn. From Disney and Pixar Animation Studios. 1 hr., 32 min. Rated PG.

articles.text: Chicken and rice soup for a cold winter’s night. Brrrr...This winter is especially chilly, often with a daily temperature range from the high- 30’s to high 40’s and for several days. Snow on the Bay Area’s highest peaks also attest to this fact. This soup can come together using ingredients you may already have on hand. Perfect for a weeknight, or busy weekend, this recipe takes less than an hour from start to table (excluding time if you prepare homemade chicken broth). I save and freeze the carcass whenever I roast a whole chicken, lately about every other week, so, it doesn’t take long before I have enough to make a couple of quarts of hearty broth. If I have immediate plans for the broth, I will season it accordingly: Asian applications will include a hefty dose of fresh ginger, turmeric, or lemongrass; otherwise, I stick with the conventional basics of onion, celery, carrots, garlic and several herbs. Once you have two quarts of broth, homemade or storebought, the rest of the soup pulls together by chopping a few more aromatics, and then simmering all the ingredients for about 30 minutes. We enjoyed our first servings with crusty garlic bread, but this soup will adapt to pretty much any serving situation. A few advance suggestions: It’s soup, so the recipe is flexible to suit your tastebuds. If using prepared chicken broth, you may want to dial up the flavor by adding a bay leaf or pinch of oregano. Greek-Inspired Chicken and Rice Soup INGREDIENTS • 8 cups chicken broth, preferably homemade but a low-sodium, prepared option works too • 1 pound chicken thighs, skinless and boneless • 1/2 cup onion, diced, about 1 • • • • • • • small 1/2 cup celery, diced 3-4 dial cloves garlic, minced 3/4 cup white rice, long-grain 1/2 cup lemon juice, freshly squeezed, or to taste 2 tablespoons olive oil Fresh parsley and/or mint leaves Freshly ground black pepper and salt, to taste INSTRUCTIONS 1. articles.text: On December 29, the last Wednesday of the year, the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group had a healthy turnout of 14 walkers, in spite of weather forecasters predicting rain. The group was pleased to welcome first-time walker Lilly Guardia Labar, who just retired from Kaiser Permanente. It was noted how much the group had grown and that there were now almost 100 people registered with the Recreation Department for the activity. Since April the group has walked almost all streets in Piedmont. However, there were a few they had not been able to get to. One was Estrella Avenue, a one-block street near Dracena Park. Walking by the new high school building, they stopped to look at the library and the not yet completed theater. High school alums Sherry Jacobs and Dick Carter told the group that the enclosed library was once an open-air quad where students had their lunches. The group passed the old carriage house used by Dress Best for Less volunteers, and viewed the architectural plans for a new aquatic center, which should be completed in 2024. The walkers continued down Bonita Avenue, enjoying the many old homes with cedar shake shingles and a beautiful old Victorian home that is one of oldest houses in Piedmont. They also saw a handsome yucca plant, an original Piedmont street lamp, and an inflatable Santa riding in an airplane with a spinning propeller that was making one of its late flights during the holiday season. At the end of Bonita, the group turned left onto Estrella Avenue, where they took a group photo. They walked down Estrella and also enjoyed the lovely homes on it, one with an interesting, cone shaped, terracotta roof above its front entrance. This is a street that gets little traffic because it runs between the more heavily traveled Moraga and Ramona Avenues. At the bottom of Estrella the street merges with Ramona Avenue. They soon found the 107- foot path between 300 and 304 Ramona that goes down to Park Way and Dracena Park. It is one of the old shortcuts that Piedmonters took to get to Key System trains during the first half of the 20th Century. Long time walkers remembered a rainy Wednesday walk about two years ago when fearless tree cutters in the park took down a set of huge, leaning eucalyptus trees that posed a threat to Park Way homes. At the bottom of Park, the street takes a 90-degree right turn and changes its name to Monticello Avenue. At that spot there is another hidden path on the left, a 169-footer that the walkers took downhill to Artuna Avenue and the panhandle of Dracena Park. Once in Dracena Park, the group inspected the surface of the children’s play area for the first time. On past visits the play structure was fully populated with small people and there was never any space for the walkers. But this past Wednesday there was only one caregiver with her charge in a carriage sitting on a nearby bench, so the group had it all to themselves. They were impressed by how soft and bouncy the surface is. They then took the path up through the park and its majestic redwood trees. A number of dogs with owners were also enjoying the beauty. The walkers stopped at Storyteller Bridge and discussed the history of the original version and its recreation by the Becker family as a Boy Scout project was told. The walkers’ weather luck finally ran out and the rain finally arrived and it was time to make a direct return to the Exedra, its starting point. It had been a year full of Walking on Wednesdays experiences, and almost all of them had been excellent, walking Piedmont’s beautiful streets and being with friends. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday, rain or shine, at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.

articles.text: Whisky. The very word invites a smile. Go ahead. Try it. Say “whisky” and watch the upward curve of the lips. Whisky is derived from usky, an eighteenth century adaptation of the Gaelic uisage beatha, which was a translation of the Latin aqua vitae, meaning “water of life.” Is it any wonder, then, that distillers proudly tout malt whisky as the result of a trinity of ingredients: barley, yeast and water? On some lighter, younger whiskies, it is possible to nose out and taste the yeasty cereal notes of the base barley. The real cornucopia of aromas and flavors – the baking spices, honey, vanilla, caramel, toffee, almonds, dried fruits, apple, pear, white flowers, chocolate shavings, ripe banana, coconut, and more – comes from the casks used for maturation. Casks open up a realm of options almost as extensive as the list of characteristics they impart. There are choices on the type of oak, size, degree to which the inside of the cask is toasted and what it was previously used to age. Most frequently, the casks used for whisky contained either bourAn inner ring of stills surrounded by an outer circle of stainless steel washbacks at Macallan is poised to help the distillery produce 11 million liters this year at the new facility, which opened to the public in June 2018. Casks, contributing approximately 80 to 85 percent of a whisky’s flavor, are being used in new ways to introduce added dimension and complexity as the “fourth” ingredient. The River Spey flows through, and gives name to, Scotland’s eastern Highland region of Speyside, arguably the country’s whisky heartland. bon or sherry. Proportions from each would be married together to create the whisky. While following the signposts along the whisky trail in Speyside of Scotland’s eastern Highlands, I quickly learned that the lineup of cask alternatives has been expanding. In the early 2000s, UK law permitted alternative casks, such as those used for brandies and fortified wines, for maturing whisky. Maturing, by definition, can be a slow and lengthy process, and we may now be seeing the results of the tinkering that occurred under a more elastic law. Based on stops for tastings, Port pipes and former cabernet sauvignon barrels seem to be the ones making their way into this mix, bringing in shades of richer fruits such as plum and dark cherry. At Dalmore, the King Alexander III is an elixir that pulls in from six different cask types, including bourbon, sherry, Port and cabernet sauvignon as well as Madeira drums and Malaga barrels. To be sure, casks have always played a central role. Many distilleries are quick to cite that 80 to 85 percent of a whisky’s flavor comes from the casks. Macallan rates the importance of the cask so highly that there is an entirely designated position for selecting the individual trees that will be used to make the casks. From the American oak, which grows taller and has smaller leaves, comes hints of butterscotch and caramel as well as lighter amber and yellow color tones. European oak, which takes longer to grow, imparts the “Christmas cake” (a popular catch-all for describing the combination of spices like nutmeg and dried fruits) and deeper red hues. Given the heavy responsibility of the casks in transmuting barley, yeast and water into the full kaleidoscope that we know as whisky, it seems an oversight to exclude them from the list of ingredients. When asked, I’ve found that the good folks working distilleries will give a nod to casks, but it’s hard to budge them on tradition and the lyricism of holding to the three raw materials. These same aficionados will then lean in and whisper the real secret ingredient, the fifth and final one: time. articles.text: A Piedmont resident for 48 years, Joyce Hart passed away peacefully on December 18. She was 88. Born Joyce Williams on June 17, 1933 at Peralta Hospital in Oakland, she was the daughter of Chester Williams and Adelaide Robbins Williams. Throughout her entire life Joyce was a true California girl. As a child she split time in both the East Bay and Southern California. She spent her school months in Orinda and Piedmont and many summers either on Mulholland Drive beneath the Hollywood sign or on an avocado orchard in Laguna Beach. Joyce attended Piedmont High School and was graduated in 1951. She moved on to UC Berkeley where she was an active member of Kappa Alpha Theta sorority. She graduated from Cal in 1955 with a degree in Public Health. Putting that education to good use, Joyce worked at Children’s Hospital in Oakland for 35 years. In 1957 Joyce married Richard (Dick) Hart and the couple began a 58 year partnership that produced sons Larry (1960), Joyce Hart, a 48-year resident of Piedmont, died on December 18 at age 88. Christopher (1969), and Jeremy (1971). Joyce was predeceased by son Kevin (1964-1967). The couple made a home on Portal Ave in Oakland until 1973 when they moved to Hillside Ave in Piedmont. The Hillside house was the center of energy and activity and many a mouth was fed over the years. Joyce enjoyed many hobbies and interests. She was a knitter, seamstress, cook, avid reader, decorator, furniture restorer, and traveler. Her two greatest passions however were bridge and Bay Area sports. articles.text: A Piedmont fire engine was sent to Taylorsville. In the background is a giant fire header. It now has become commonplace to have enormous wildfires every summer in California to the extent that summer and fall are called “fire season.” 2021’s fire season may not have seemed as bad as 2020, since last year’s devastation of wooded lands occurred further away from the eye of Bay Area. However, it was one of the most destructive in recorded California history. For Piedmont firefighters, the 2021 fire season again called upon them to lend a helping hand. Piedmont fire crews were deployed to fight the enormous Dixie Fire in Janesville, Lassen County, on July 20. They stayed battling the flames with five crew rotations, each one lasting 7-10 days. Piedmont crews were also sent to Taylorsville to protect the town. The Dixie Fire burned for three and a half months through Butte, Plumas, Lassen, Shasta, and Tehama Counties from July 13 to October 25 and consumed 963,309 acres before rain helped fire crews fully contain the blaze. “As a firefighter in these very intense fire seasons, it is critical that we send available resources throughout the state as there simply aren’t enough people or apparatus to fight every fire. We will absolutely need mutual aid to be reciprocated when we have fires in Piedmont, so we’re proud to be able to serve when called,” said Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. The Dixie fire was the largest single origin (non-complex) fire in California history. Only the August Lightning Complex fire in 2020 was larger with over 1,032,648 acres. The fire was begun by 38 separate dry lighting-induced fires. Yesterady, Cal Fire officials concluded that the Dixie fire was started by PG&E power lines. When a minor power outage was detected July 13 in the Feather River Canyon near Cresta Dam, a single PG&E maintenance worker responded. The worker was delayed by bridge repairs blocking his route. The worker arrived nine and half hours later to find a fallen tree on a live power line that had started a small brush fire. He attempted to extinguish it by himself, but without success. Cal Fire sent aircraft to drop water on the fire but an illegal drone appeared over the fire, endangering the aircraft and forcing a premature halt to helicopter operations which may have “played a major part in the blaze burning out of control after darkness fell,” according to Butte County District Attorney Mike Ramsey. The ongoing drought in California contributed to a total of 8,619 fires during 2021, and resulted in 2,569,009 acres burned. Other 2021 fires include the Monument fire ever in Trinity County which was the 14th largest California fire at 223,124 acres, and the Caldor fire in Alpine, Amador and El Dorado counties with 221,835 acres burned. Last year, 2021, proved to be the second largest fire year in California’s history, and only one year after the all-time largest year of 4,397,809 acres destroyed in 2020. The Dixie Fire burns near Milford in Lassen County on August 17, 2021.

articles.text: An epic snowstorm hitting Lake Tahoe near the end of December has resulted in a record 214 inches of snow – nearly 18 feet – in less than a month. As a favorite vacation destination for Piedmont residents, Tahoe provided a white Christmas, but resulted in road closures of Highways 80. 50, 267 and SR 28 for more than three days. Hundreds of families were unable to return home due to the highway closures. The snow measured at Donner Pass by U.C. Berkeley’s Central Sierra Snow Lab revealed that the total is higher than any other December in 142 years when snowfall was first recorded in Tahoe. The Snow Lab reports that the current snowfall is at 242% of the average snowfall for 2021- 2022. Rains in October helped prepare the Tahoe landscape for potential runoff in the future. At Northstar Ski Resort, 134 inches of snow – more than 11 feet – fell in a 7-day period, from December 22-28. The biggest amount was at Donner Pass with 36 inches in one day – December 27. The record at Donner Pass is 52 inches that fell in one day in 1989. Piedmont residents trying to drive back to the East Bay reported seeing snow to the tops of telephone poles. Snowfall measures the cumulative daily of snow falling, while snowpack differs and is the amount of snow that remains after melting. The snowpack in the Sierras is at 150% of average as of January 4. Climatologist and California Department of Water Resources (CDWR) Officials agree that the current drought is not over. “December alone will not end the drought, clearly,” said Jeanine Jones, interstate resources manager for CDWR. Climatologists are predicting dry conditions for the rest of the season. Models predict the second straight year of La Niña, which deflects storms in the Pacific to the Northwest and can mean drier conditions in the Southwest of North America. California adopted new emergency drought regulations on January 4 to conserve water. The regulations ban using hoses to clean sidewalks and driveways, washing cars without a shutoff nozzle on the hose and watering lawns and gardens after rain. Cars drive slowly through mountainous walls of snow. Travel to and from Tahoe was made difficult or impossible on Highways 80, 50, 267 and SR 28, all of which were closed the days following Christmas. The record for most Tahoe snowfall in a month in the last 30 years was 238 inches in January 2017. December 2021’s storms produced 214 inches of snow, two feet shy of the record.

articles.text: The new year has brought with it a familiar trend ­ – event postponements and cancellations due to a rise in COVID cases. On December 30, the Piedmont Recreation Department’s inaugural “Noon Year’s Eve” event was cancelled, citing the recent spike in COVID cases. The Department also announced that its preschool open house, originally scheduled to be in-person on Saturday, January 8, would instead be held virtually. The Piedmont Community Church has also switched gears to offer only virtual worship services for January 9 and 16. “From what we are gathering, the worst of the spike of COVID cases will occur in the next two to three weeks and then the number of cases will decrease as quickly as they increased,” said Rev. Dr. Steve Schibsted of Piedmont Community Church. “We do not think it is wise to return to in-person worship during the biggest surge of COVID since we began this journey almost two years ago. As the surge abates, we will decide the best Sunday to return to in-person worship.” All city public meetings will now be held virtually during the month of January, to include City Council, committee and commission meetings.

pages.text: 28 Wednesday, January 5, 2022 COVID surge results in event cancellations By Allyson Aleksey The new year has brought with it a familiar trend ­ – event postponements and cancellations due to a rise in COVID cases. On December 30, the Piedmont Recreation Department’s inaugural “Noon Year’s Eve” event was cancelled, citing the recent spike in COVID cases. The Department also announced that its preschool open house, originally scheduled to be in-person on Saturday, January 8, would instead be held virtually. The Piedmont Community Church has also switched gears to offer only virtual worship services for January 9 and 16. “From what we are gathering, the worst of the spike of COVID cases will occur in the next two to three weeks and then the number of cases will decrease as quickly as they increased,” said Rev. Dr. Steve Schibsted of Piedmont Community Church. “We do not think it is wise to return to in-person worship during the biggest surge of COVID since we began this journey almost two years ago. As the surge abates, we will decide the best Sunday to return to in-person worship.” All city public meetings will now be held virtually during the month of January, to include City Council, committee and commission meetings. Boys’ varsity coach Todd Sullivan confirmed that PHS teams will be able to play at least three home games this week and next at Alameda Point and Estuary Park in Alameda. “Recent heavy rains caused subbase materials to shift and turf material to stretch and tear resulting in holes, ridges and elevation changes that present significant tripping hazards,” Communications Director Brian Killgore stated in a December 17 press release. Nearly two weeks ago the school district requested emergency repairs by FieldTurf which was to send a crew to assess the scope of work. “The turf will be peeled back to restore and level the subbase materials, cut out and replace damaged sections of the turf, and glue the turf back into place,” according to the district. In 2018, Director of Facilities Pete Palmer explained the plan to fix the drainage would cost between $4 and $5 million. Palmer cited ADA regulations requiring ramps for wheelchairs as a factor in the high price tag. The original field and installation in 2000 cost $800,000. The recent plan for repair was to dig a 2 to 3-foot trench around the inside perimeter of the track. In 2019 when repairs to the field were officially delayed, Superintendent Booker said funds were tied up in the H1 Bond constructing the STEAM and new theater buildings.
